claims.claim: Once profiling has identified an edit family, searching a small upstream source repository for the measured mechanism and inspecting exact files is a valid way to find candidate implementations.

evidence.observation: The pinned repository contains compact, mechanism-specific examples whose exact paths can be inspected after a profiler has narrowed the candidate class.
The repository is a small set of direct ldmatrix/stmatrix instruction examples rather than a general optimization authority.

challenge.alternative: The source cards alone are sufficient implementation evidence, so exact upstream files do not need inspection.
challenge.check: Compare the source-card summaries with the pinned repository file trees and implementations.
challenge.outcome: Several source-card architecture and mechanism labels exceed the code's actual scope, while exact files discriminate what is present.

claims.claim: The displayed clone-and-grep snippet is reproducible enough to support exact implementation citations.

evidence.observation: The snippet clones the moving default branch and records neither this immutable revision nor an exact file; future results can change.
This repository only demonstrates ldmatrix/stmatrix, so the shared broad regular expression does not establish the page's wider TMA, swizzle, Stream-K, or vector-width scope.

claims.claim: Load/store and transpose examples are relevant candidate sources after profiling identifies long-scoreboard or sector-utilization symptoms, without proving that vector width or layout is the cause.

evidence.observation: The pinned SM90a examples compare TMA transpose variants and explicitly encode 128-byte tensor-map swizzling.
The source tree contains direct coalescing and shared-memory transpose examples, including a bank-conflict-free padded layout.

challenge.alternative: Those profiler symptoms uniquely diagnose a layout or vector-width defect.
challenge.check: Inspect whether the repositories define profiler-counter causality or instead provide candidate mechanisms.
challenge.outcome: They provide implementation examples but no symptom-to-cause theorem; the page only recommends searching before editing.

claims.claim: The Colfax repositories contain Hopper pipelined GEMM and TMA/barrier examples relevant to investigating barrier or TMA-wait stalls before changing stages or producer/consumer roles.

evidence.observation: The pinned files implement SM90 TMA copies, transaction barriers, multistage GEMM, and a warp-specialized alternative.
The source documents and implements SM90a software pipelining with optional warp specialization and CUTLASS PipelineTmaAsync.

challenge.alternative: The examples establish that changing stage count or role split will improve any kernel with these stalls.
challenge.check: Inspect the stated target/version and configuration scope of each example.
challenge.outcome: The sources are Hopper-specific candidate implementations and make no portable performance guarantee; the page says to search them before changing code.

claims.claim: The pinned cfx repository contains persistent data-parallel and Stream-K schedulers relevant to investigating tail waves before adding shape-specific dispatch.

evidence.locator: tile_scheduler.hpp classes and cli_options.h scheduler values
evidence.observation: The source implements SingleTileScheduler, DataParallelPersistentTileScheduler, and StreamKPersistentTileScheduler, selectable as non-persistent, persistent, Stream-K, or heuristic modes.

challenge.alternative: A tail wave proves that a persistent or Stream-K scheduler is the best fix.
challenge.check: Inspect whether the repository connects profiler tail metrics to a universal scheduler choice.
challenge.outcome: It exposes alternatives and shape controls rather than a universal choice; the page treats them as candidates to inspect.

claims.claim: Citing a local source page plus an exact upstream path, commit, or URL is sufficient implementation provenance.

evidence.observation: Evidence must record a revision and an exact section, symbol, line, or table locator; a moving repository URL by itself is insufficient.
The local summary assigns SM100 and persistent/tile-scheduling scope although the pinned source is SM90a and contains no such implementation, demonstrating why the source page is only a lead.

claims.claim: The linked repositories provide TMA, swizzle, Stream-K, persistence, and load/store mechanics on both Hopper- and Blackwell-era kernels.

evidence.locator: pipeline-gemm, streamk, tma and transpose-cute build files/source symbols
evidence.observation: The relevant modern examples compile for SM90a and use SM90 TMA/GMMA facilities; no SM100 target or tcgen05 implementation appears.

evidence.locator: FMHA READMEs, compile scripts and CUTLASS GEMM source
evidence.observation: The repository explicitly targets Hopper SM90/SM90a with CUDA 12.2/12.3 and SM90 TMA/WGMMA.
The repository calls itself a Hopper transpose example and compiles with -arch=sm_90a.
The repository is six ldmatrix/stmatrix examples compiled for sm_90a, not a Blackwell source map.

commands: git ls-remote each linked repository and inspect pinned shallow clones
rg exact architecture, mechanism and scheduler symbols in each pinned tree
scope: All nine baseline body units, frontmatter architecture claims, and all five linked source-card scopes were checked against exact upstream repository revisions.
residual_risk: No GPU benchmark was run. The verified workflow claims are candidate-discovery rules, not claims that a profiler symptom proves a root cause or that a transferred implementation improves performance.
